newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rubin sees gold sales, prices under control - paper.
newsitem.headline: Rubin sees gold sales, prices under control - paper.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin predicted in an interview published on Wednesday the IMF would sell part of its gold reserves and said inflation in the U.S. and other G7 countries is "not reigniting."

Rubin told the International Herald Tribune that despite opposition from Germany, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) would have to sell as much as US$2 billion of its gold reserves to help finance an aid plan for the world's poorest debtor nations.
"Ultimately I think some small portion of gold will have to be sold. I can't help it if there is a difference in view," the newspaper quoted him as saying.
Rubin also said: "I think the probability is extremely high that we will have continued growth in the U.S. economy with low inflation."
He added that "as you look around the world, the evidence suggests that inflation is not reigniting in the U.S. and beyond the U.S. in the rest of the G7," the newspaper reported.
Rubin was talking ahead of a Group of Seven finance ministers meeting and the annual IMF meeting in Washington.

In a temporary face-saving compromise, the IMF's executive board last week put off for the time being a decision on the sale of gold, which would help fund part of an expected $6 billion package of aid for about a dozen African nations.

The newspaper quoted aides to Rubin in Washington as saying the U.S. would be prepared to make a financial contribution to the IMF's structual adjustment facility, but only if accompanied by plans for gold sales.
Other points made by Rubin in the Herald Tribune interview included:

* Enormous progress has made on plans to double, to $50 billion, the General Arrangements to Borrow, a special credit line established by a group of wealthy countries to assist the IMF in times of crisis.

* The United States and China are planning to hold a meeting of the Joint Economic Commission of finance ministers and other officials in Washington, probably in late November, to discuss economic issues of importance to Beijing and Washington.

* Rubin and Alan Greenspan, the chairman of the Federal Reserve Board, will welcome finance ministers and central bankers from members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to Washington next Wednesday for a meeting that shows "the importance of Asian nations in the world economy."
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
* One of the main reasons the United States is creating more jobs than Europe is that it has more flexible capital and labour markets.
